questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nehru's Foreign Policy' refers to.
questions.a: Jawaharlal Nehru, as India's first Prime Minister and the architect of its foreign policy, shaped the country's international relations on the principles of anti-colonialism, anti-imperialism, anti-racism, peaceful coexistence and friendship with all nations. He believed that foreign policy should be an extension of the values of the freedom struggle.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nehru's Foreign Policy'.
questions.a: Nehru's foreign policy rested on five core principles: (1) anti-colonialism and support for the independence of colonised peoples; (2) anti-racism and opposition to apartheid; (3) peaceful coexistence and resolution of disputes through dialogue; (4) friendship with all countries and alliances with none; (5) respect for sovereignty and non-interference. Nehru personally held the External Affairs portfolio for most of his tenure and gave Indian foreign policy a distinct moral and idealist orientation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nehru's Foreign Policy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Nehru's Foreign Policy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Non-alignment' refers to.
questions.a: Non-alignment is the cornerstone of India's foreign policy during the Cold War. It meant that India would not join either of the two military blocs -- the US-led Western alliance or the Soviet-led Eastern bloc -- and would instead pursue an independent foreign policy based on national interest and judging each issue on its merits.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Non-alignment'.
questions.a: Non-alignment was not neutrality or isolationism; it was an active and independent stance. Its key features: (1) India refused to join any military alliance or bloc; (2) India retained the freedom to take independent positions on international issues; (3) India could accept economic or technical aid from both blocs; (4) it became the basis of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), founded at the Bandung Conference (1955) and the first NAM summit in Belgrade (1961); (5) it helped newly independent countries of Asia and Africa maintain their autonomy in a bipolar world.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Non-alignment' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Non-alignment

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India and the Cold War' refers to.
questions.a: During the Cold War, the world was divided into two rival military blocs led by the United States and the Soviet Union. India, through non-alignment, refused to join either bloc and maintained equidistance, while accepting economic and technical aid from both sides and taking independent positions on global issues.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India and the Cold War'.
questions.a: India's Cold War policy had several dimensions: (1) it stayed out of both military alliances (NATO and the Warsaw Pact); (2) it accepted aid from both the US and the USSR -- e.g. PL-480 wheat from the US and steel plants and defence equipment from the USSR; (3) it tilted towards the USSR on some issues while maintaining overall independence; (4) it used NAM to mediate between the blocs and promote disarmament; (5) the policy allowed India to protect its strategic autonomy despite pressures from both superpowers.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India and the Cold War' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India and the Cold War

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India-China Relations' refers to.
questions.a: India-China relations began with great warmth after both became republics in the late 1940s. India was among the first countries to recognise the People's Republic of China (1950) and championed China's entry into the UN. The relationship was symbolised by the slogan 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai' and the Panchsheel (Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence) agreement of 1954, but deteriorated due to the border dispute and the 1962 war.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India-China Relations'.
questions.a: The evolution of India-China relations: (1) 1950 -- India recognised the PRC; (2) 1954 -- Panchsheel agreement (mutual respect for territorial integrity, non-aggression, non-interference, equality, peaceful coexistence); (3) the border dispute over the Aksai Chin and NEFA regions; (4) the Tibet issue and the Dalai Lama's asylum in India (1959); (5) the 1962 war that ended the era of friendship; (6) the relationship remained strained for decades before gradual normalisation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India-China Relations' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India-China Relations

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The 1962 India-China War' refers to.
questions.a: The 1962 India-China war was a brief but decisive border conflict fought along the Himalayan frontier. It arose from the unresolved border dispute over Aksai Chin (in the west) and the North East Frontier Agency (NEFA, in the east), differing perceptions of the McMahon Line, and the fallout of the Tibet issue. The war ended with a Chinese unilateral ceasefire and left a deep imprint on India's foreign and defence policy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The 1962 India-China War'.
questions.a: Key aspects of the 1962 war: (1) causes -- the border dispute over Aksai Chin and NEFA, China's rejection of the McMahon Line, and the Tibet fallout; (2) course -- Chinese forces advanced into Indian territory in both sectors in October-November 1962; (3) outcome -- China declared a unilateral ceasefire and withdrew from NEFA but retained Aksai Chin; (4) impact -- it was a humiliating defeat for India, led to the resignation of Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon, accelerated India's defence modernisation, and shook confidence in non-alignment.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The 1962 India-China War' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The 1962 India-China War

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India-Pakistan Wars' refers to.
questions.a: India and Pakistan fought three major wars -- in 1947-48, 1965 and 1971 -- arising primarily from the unresolved dispute over Jammu and Kashmir and, in 1971, from the crisis in East Pakistan (Bangladesh). The 1971 war resulted in the creation of Bangladesh and a decisive Indian victory.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India-Pakistan Wars'.
questions.a: The three India-Pakistan wars: (1) 1947-48 -- fought over Kashmir after tribal infiltration from Pakistan; ended with a UN-mediated ceasefire and the CFL; (2) 1965 -- Pakistan launched Operation Gibraltar to foment rebellion in Kashmir; India retaliated across the Punjab border; ended with the Tashkent Declaration (1966); (3) 1971 -- sparked by the Bangladesh liberation crisis; India intervened after the refugee influx; ended with the surrender of Pakistani forces in Dhaka and the creation of Bangladesh; followed by the Shimla Agreement (1972).

questions.q: Under which section is 'India-Pakistan Wars' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India-Pakistan Wars

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India and its Neighbours' refers to.
questions.a: India shares land or maritime borders with several countries in South Asia -- Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and the Maldives. India's neighbourhood policy has aimed at building friendly, cooperative relations while managing disputes and asymmetries arising from India's size and power in the region.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India and its Neighbours'.
questions.a: India's relations with its neighbours: (1) Nepal and Bhutan -- close cultural and economic ties, open borders (with Nepal), and security cooperation; (2) Bangladesh -- born with India's help in 1971, with cooperation on water-sharing and border issues; (3) Sri Lanka -- affected by the Tamil question and India's intervention (IPKF, 1987-90); (4) Pakistan and China -- strained by the Kashmir and border disputes; (5) the Gujral Doctrine (1990s) of unilateral accommodation with smaller neighbours; (6) SAARC as a regional cooperation framework.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India and its Neighbours' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India and its Neighbours

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India's Nuclear Policy' refers to.
questions.a: India's nuclear policy evolved from an early commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy and global disarmament to the development of nuclear weapons. India refused to sign the discriminatory Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), conducted the Pokhran-I (1974) 'peaceful nuclear explosion' and the Pokhran-II (1998) nuclear tests, and subsequently adopted a policy of credible minimum deterrence with a no-first-use commitment.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India's Nuclear Policy'.
questions.a: Key elements of India's nuclear policy: (1) early emphasis on peaceful uses of nuclear energy under Homi Bhabha; (2) strong advocacy of global nuclear disarmament; (3) refusal to sign the NPT (1968) as it was discriminatory between nuclear and non-nuclear states; (4) Pokhran-I (1974) peaceful nuclear explosion under Indira Gandhi; (5) Pokhran-II (1998) weaponisation tests under Vajpayee, making India a nuclear-weapon state; (6) adoption of a no-first-use doctrine and credible minimum deterrence; (7) the Indo-US civil nuclear agreement (2005-08).

questions.q: Under which section is 'India's Nuclear Policy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India's Nuclear Policy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Disarmament and India's Role' refers to.
questions.a: Disarmament refers to the reduction or elimination of weapons, especially weapons of mass destruction (nuclear, chemical and biological), through international agreements. India has been a consistent advocate of global nuclear disarmament, arguing that complete, universal and non-discriminatory disarmament is the only way to ensure genuine international security.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Disarmament and India's Role'.
questions.a: India's role in disarmament: (1) it championed the cause of nuclear disarmament at the UN from the 1950s; (2) it proposed the Rajiv Gandhi Action Plan (1988) for time-bound, universal nuclear disarmament; (3) it opposed the discriminatory NPT and CTBT (Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, 1996) as they did not include time-bound disarmament by nuclear-weapon states; (4) it supported treaties banning chemical and biological weapons; (5) it argued that disarmament must be universal, non-discriminatory and verifiable, not selective.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Disarmament and India's Role' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Disarmament and India's Role
